title: "Vector Databases and Embeddings"

## What is an embedding?

An **embedding** is a numerical representation of data — text, an image, a
sound clip — as a list of numbers called a **vector**. It's an AI technique
that converts a word, a sentence, or a whole document into a long string of
numbers, and you can think of those numbers as coordinates on a massive,
multidimensional map.

Imagine a map of the world: Cairo and Alexandria sit close together because
they're physically close. An embedding model does the same thing, but for
*meaning* instead of geography. The words "King" and "Queen" land at nearly
the same coordinates because they both represent royalty. "I'm feeling down"
and "I am sad" sit right next to each other even though the two sentences
don't share a single word. Concretely, "King" might embed as `[0.12, -0.45,
0.78, ..., 0.33]` (384 numbers long, for a typical small embedding model) and
"Queen" as `[0.14, -0.43, 0.77, ..., 0.31]` — the vectors are close because
the meanings are close. **Semantic similarity equals distance proximity.**

Embeddings capture *relationships*, not just definitions. The classic
word2vec example: in embedding space, `"Paris" - "France" + "Italy"` lands
very close to `"Rome"`. In short: an embedding turns a human concept into a
mathematical location.

## What is a vector database?

A traditional database — a spreadsheet, a SQL table — is built for exact
matches: look up a specific order ID, a specific phone number. Ask it to
"find documents about a happy puppy" and it has to scan every row of text
looking for those literal words, missing anything phrased as "a joyful young
dog." That's slow, and it's blind to meaning.

A **vector database** is built differently. It stores the embeddings
themselves — those long coordinate strings — and when you ask it a question,
it doesn't read the text at all. It converts your question into a coordinate,
drops that point onto the map, and asks: *what are the closest items
surrounding this point?* This is called **similarity search** or **nearest
neighbor search**, and because it relies on geometry rather than reading text
line by line, a vector database can search billions of documents in
milliseconds.

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    Q["Your question"] --> E["Embedding model"]
    E --> V["Query vector"]
    V --> DB[("Vector database<br>(indexed embeddings)")]
    DB --> R["Nearest-neighbor matches"]
```

Purpose-built, a vector database exists to do three things: store millions or
billions of embedding vectors, index them with algorithms like **HNSW**
(Hierarchical Navigable Small World) so search stays fast at scale, and answer
a query by embedding it with the *same* model used on the stored documents,
then finding its nearest neighbors.

### How the search actually runs, in three steps

1. **Indexing (preparation).** Before any query arrives, the database builds
   a graph or clustering structure over every stored vector, so it never has
   to brute-force scan the whole collection later. Common index types: HNSW
   (a layered graph) and IVF (clusters vectors into buckets, like a phonebook
   divided by city).
2. **Querying (search).** Your text query is embedded with the same model
   used at indexing time, then the system asks which stored vectors are
   closest to that query vector, using a distance metric.
3. **Retrieval (result).** The database returns the top-*k* most similar
   items — say, the top 5 chunks — which are then handed to the LLM in a RAG
   system to generate an answer.

### Distance metrics

| Metric | What it measures | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Cosine similarity | Angle between vectors (ignores magnitude) | Text embeddings, where document length shouldn't dominate |
| Euclidean distance | Straight-line distance | Low-dimensional, numeric data |
| Dot product | Magnitude × direction | When vector length matters (e.g., recommendation scores) |

Cosine similarity is the default for text: it ranges from −1 (opposite
meaning) to +1 (identical meaning), and two vectors pointing the same
direction score as highly similar even if one document is much longer than
the other.

### A concrete worked example

Suppose a vector database stores three sentences, each reduced here to a
simplified 3-dimensional embedding for illustration:

| ID | Text | Embedding (simplified 3D) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | "The sky is blue" | `[0.9, 0.1, 0.2]` |
| 2 | "Grass is green" | `[0.1, 0.9, 0.1]` |
| 3 | "The ocean is deep" | `[0.8, 0.2, 0.3]` |

A query about the sky would embed close to `[0.9, 0.1, 0.2]`, land nearest to
sentence 1, and land second-nearest to sentence 3 — "the ocean is deep" — not
because the words overlap, but because both sentences describe a
similarly-colored, similarly-toned natural scene. Sentence 2 sits far away in
this tiny 3D space, exactly like "grass is green" is a different topic.
Real embedding models don't use 3 dimensions — they typically use hundreds —
but the geometry works identically at scale.

### Why this matters

Without vector databases and embeddings, LLMs have two structural flaws: they
**forget** (a fixed context window can't hold a company's entire knowledge
base) and they **hallucinate** (when unsure, they guess plausibly rather than
admit ignorance). A vector database gives an LLM the equivalent of an
open-book exam — instead of relying purely on what it memorized during
training, it can look up the exact relevant passage first, then answer from
that. This pairing is exactly what RAG (covered on the [next
page](02_advanced_rag_engineering.qmd)) is built on.

## Document indexing: two different layers

"Indexing" gets used loosely, but in a vector database context it actually
refers to two separate layers: how chunks are **logically** organized so the
LLM gets the cleanest context, and how vectors are **physically** stored so
the search itself is fast. Chunking (splitting documents into pieces) happens
*before* indexing; indexing is what the database does with those chunks once
it has them.

### Logical / data indexing strategies

These strategies decide how retrieved text connects back to its source, to
maximize what the LLM actually sees:

- **Single-level (flat) indexing.** The simplest style — every chunk is an
  independent vector, and the system fetches the top matches and passes them
  straight to the LLM.
- **Parent-child (hierarchical) indexing.** Small child chunks (sentences)
  are indexed for precision search, but each is linked to a larger parent
  chunk (a paragraph). The system searches the precise child vectors but
  returns the more context-rich parent text to the LLM.
- **Hypothetical question indexing.** An LLM pre-reads every document and
  generates several questions a user might plausibly ask about it. Those
  *questions* — not the raw text — are what gets embedded and indexed. A
  real user question then matches against a question that's phrased the way
  users actually phrase things.
- **Summary / document indexing.** Instead of indexing raw paragraphs, an LLM
  writes a high-level summary of each whole document. The system searches
  summaries first to find the right document, then drills into that
  document's specific chunks.
- **Knowledge graph indexing.** Extracts entities as nodes and relationships
  as edges, so the system can answer questions that require connecting facts
  scattered across separate documents — something flat chunk retrieval can't
  do on its own.

### Physical / algorithmic indexing strategies

These are the actual **Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)** algorithms —
trading a small amount of mathematical precision for a large gain in search
speed:

| Strategy | Accuracy | Speed | Memory | Training required? | Use case |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flat (no index) | Exact | Very slow — O(N) | Low | No | Under 10K vectors |
| IVF | Approximate | Fast | Moderate | Yes (k-means) | 100K–10M vectors |
| HNSW | Very high | Very fast | High | No | Up to millions, when accuracy matters |
| PQ | Approximate | Fast | Very low | Yes (codebooks) | Memory-constrained environments |
| IVF+PQ | Good | Very fast | Very low | Yes | Large-scale, 100M+ vectors |
| ScaNN | Very high | Extremely fast | Moderate | Yes | Performance-critical, Google-scale |

- **Flat** brute-forces the exact distance to every vector — perfect
  accuracy, but only viable on tiny collections.
- **IVF** (Inverted File Index) clusters the vector space with k-means into
  "buckets" (Voronoi cells); a query only searches the bucket its own vector
  falls closest to, at the cost of some accuracy.
- **HNSW** builds a multi-layer graph, like an express subway line — the
  search takes big leaps across the top layer, then drops down layers to
  fine-tune the exact match. It's what Pinecone, Weaviate, and ChromaDB use
  by default.
- **PQ** (Product Quantization) compresses each vector into small
  approximate sub-vector codes, shrinking memory by up to 95% — often paired
  with IVF as **IVF-PQ** for billion-scale collections.
- **ScaNN**, Google's index, optimizes anisotropic vector distances to
  favor vectors that align cleanly with the query's direction, for
  hyper-scale production search.

A simple decision path: under 10K vectors, use Flat (no training, exact).
Need over 99% accuracy and have the RAM for it, use HNSW. Have over 10M
vectors and limited RAM, use IVF+PQ. Operating at Google scale, consider
ScaNN.

### Tuning HNSW: precision vs. speed

Since HNSW is the default in most production vector databases (Pinecone,
Weaviate, ChromaDB), its three parameters are worth knowing by name:

- **`M`** — bi-directional links per node. Higher `M` means better recall
  but more memory (typical range: 16–64).
- **`ef_construction`** — candidate list size while the index is being
  built. Higher means a better-quality index, but a slower build.
- **`ef` (search)** — candidate list size at query time. Higher means better
  recall but slower search — this is the one you tune per query, at runtime.

The trade-off is concrete: `ef=10` is fast but only around 85% recall;
`ef=200` is slow but around 99% recall. Rule of thumb: tune `M` and
`ef_construction` once, at build time; tune `ef` per query's latency budget,
at runtime.

## Semantic search and similarity search

**Keyword search** — the traditional approach — matches exact words or
substrings: `LIKE` clauses, inverted indexes, boolean logic. A query for
"car" retrieves only documents containing the literal string "car." Search
for "canine therapy" on a site whose articles only say "dog healing," and you
get zero results, even though the content is exactly what you wanted. Keyword
search is blind to meaning: it misses synonyms ("automobile" vs. "car"),
misses context (is "Jaguar" an animal, a car, or an OS?), word order matters
in brittle ways, and it breaks on polysemy — one word, many meanings.

**Semantic search** understands the *intent* behind a query rather than its
literal words. "Ways to calm a nervous dog" retrieves documents about
"reducing canine anxiety" or "soothing an agitated pet" even though none of
those exact words match. It handles synonyms, concept matching ("cold
weather" ↔ "winter conditions"), and phrasing variation ("How do I…" ↔ "What
is the method for…"). Semantic search is conceptual: it maps queries and
documents into a shared meaning space.

**Similarity search** is the mathematical engine underneath semantic search —
not a linguistic operation at all, but a geometric one: given a target vector,
find every stored vector close to it by some distance metric. A useful
non-text analogy: imagine a room of people, each with an age and a height —
Alice (25, 160cm), Bob (26, 162cm), Carol (45, 170cm), Dave (46, 172cm). Ask
"find people similar to Alice" and a keyword match fails outright (no one
else is named Alice), but plotting age against height and measuring distance
immediately shows that Bob is close to Alice, while Carol and Dave — close to
*each other* but far from Alice — are not similar to her. Vector databases do
exactly this, just across hundreds of dimensions instead of two.

Concretely, this runs in three steps. First, **embedding**: both the query
and every stored document are converted into vectors with the same embedding
model — e.g., the query "happy dog" might embed as `[0.9, 0.1, 0.8]`, a
document "joyful puppy" as `[0.88, 0.12, 0.79]` (very close), and a document
"sad cat" as `[0.2, 0.9, 0.1]` (far away). Second, **distance calculation**:
pick a metric — cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, or dot product (see
the table above) — and score every stored vector against the query vector.
Third, **nearest-neighbor search**: find the top-*k* stored vectors with the
highest similarity. A brute-force search compares the query against every
single stored vector — accurate, but too slow once there are millions of
them — so in practice vector databases use **Approximate Nearest Neighbor
(ANN)** indexing (HNSW, IVF) to find "good enough" neighbors in
milliseconds instead.

For example, a user searching "steps to fix a flat tire" shows the gap
directly:

| Feature | Keyword search (old school) | Semantic / similarity search (modern) |
|---|---|---|
| How it searches | Scans literal strings of text characters | Converts the query to a vector; finds nearest-neighbor vectors |
| What it finds | Only documents containing the exact words "fix," "flat," and "tire" | Documents about "changing a punctured wheel" or "replacing a blown tire," even without those exact words |
| Flaw | Misses relevant documents that use different vocabulary | Needs more compute and a purpose-built vector database |

### Summary

| Concept | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Embedding | A list of numbers (vector) that captures the meaning of data |
| Vector database | A database optimized to search millions of embeddings by similarity, not exact match |
| Distance metric | A mathematical way to measure similarity (cosine, Euclidean, dot product) |
| Index (e.g., HNSW) | A pre-built structure that speeds up nearest-neighbor search dramatically |
| Use case | Powering LLM retrieval (RAG), semantic search, recommendations |
